title: When calls fail: timeouts, backoff, idempotency and circuit breakers
dek: Every call over a network can fail, stall or succeed without the caller finding out. Designs that survive this have the same few habits: give up after a deadline, retry with growing and randomised waits, make retried writes harmless, and stop calling a service that is clearly down. Interviewers ask about these to see whether you've run real systems.

items: Assume the network fails. Set a timeout on every call; retry only what is safe to repeat; back off exponentially with jitter so retries don't arrive all at once.
A retried write must not happen twice: give each operation an idempotency key, and have the server record keys and return the first result for a repeat.
A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing, fails fast with a fallback, and tests it again after a pause, so one sick service doesn't take the rest down.
The request is lost, or the server crashes before answering: the caller hears nothing.
The server is slow: overloaded, garbage collecting, waiting on its own slow dependency.
The work succeeds but the response is lost. This is the dangerous one: the caller can't tell it from a failure.
The call fails fast with an error: connection refused, 503, 429.
Partial failure: one replica is bad, one zone is cut off, one in a hundred calls fails.

body.x: 'The network is reliable' is the first of the well-known fallacies of distributed computing. A design that assumes every call returns promptly will hang, overload or double-charge on the first bad night.

A call with no timeout can wait forever, holding a thread, a connection and the user. Every network call needs one, set from what the caller can afford, not from how long the call usually takes: if the order screen must load in 2 seconds, the call to the menu service might get 300 ms. Separate the time to connect (short: a healthy server accepts in milliseconds) from the time to answer.

Deadlines are better still: the first service sets a deadline for the whole request, and each call passes on what is left. Then a service three calls deep stops working on a request the user gave up on long ago. gRPC does this for you.
Many failures are brief: a packet lost, a server restarting, a moment of overload. Trying again usually works. But retries are also how a small problem becomes a large one.

body.cap: Retrying at once, or on a fixed schedule, turns a struggling service's failures into synchronised waves of extra load. Exponential backoff reduces how many retries there are; jitter spreads them out so they never arrive together.

items: Backoff: wait before retrying, and wait longer each time: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, up to a cap.
Jitter: randomise each wait, for example pick anything between zero and the backoff time. Without it, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment.
Limit attempts (three is common) and keep a retry budget, for instance retries may add at most 10% to normal traffic; past that, fail.
Retry only what is safe to repeat and only failures that might be temporary: timeouts, 503, 429 (honouring `Retry-After`). A 400 or 403 will fail the same way again.
Retry at one layer. If the app, the gateway and each service all retry three times, one failure deep in the stack becomes 27 calls.

body.x: In an interview, 'retry with exponential backoff and jitter' is the phrase to use, and being able to explain why jitter matters is what separates senior answers.

A retried GET is harmless. A retried 'charge ₹349' is not: if the first attempt worked and only its reply was lost, the customer pays twice. The fix is to make the operation idempotent, so that doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.

body.cap: The key names this payment attempt, not the request. The retry carries the same key, so Payments recognises it and returns the result it already has instead of charging again.

items: The client creates an idempotency key for each logical operation (a payment for order 9101, attempt 1) and sends it with every retry of that operation.

The server stores the key with the result before or as it does the work, in the same transaction where possible. A repeat with a finished key gets the stored result; a repeat while the first is still running waits for it or gets 409 'in progress'.
Keys can be natural: one rating per user per order means `user 77 + order 9101` is already a key. Unique constraints in the database then refuse the duplicate.
Keep keys for as long as retries can happen (a day is common), then let them expire.
Payment providers such as Razorpay and Stripe accept an idempotency key for exactly this reason; pass yours through.

body.x: When a dependency is down, timeouts and retries still cost something: every call waits for its timeout, threads pile up, and the retries add load to a service that is trying to recover. A database coming back after a crash can be flattened by the backlog of retries and fall over again, again and again.

body.cap: The breaker watches the calls. When too many fail it stops calling for a while and answers at once with a fallback, then lets a single test call decide whether to resume.

items: Closed: calls go through and failures are counted over a short window.

Open: once failures pass a threshold (say half of the calls in 10 seconds), calls fail immediately without being made. The caller uses a fallback: Dispatch shows an arrival time from distance alone; the menu shows its last cached version; a recommendation strip is hidden.
Half-open: after a pause (say 30 seconds), one test call is allowed. Success closes the breaker; failure opens it again for another pause.
Benefits: the caller fails fast instead of hanging, the struggling service gets room to recover, and users see a degraded feature instead of an error page.

body.x: Put breakers around calls to third-party APIs (maps, SMS, payments), around each downstream service, and around anything slow or expensive. Libraries and service meshes provide them; you choose the thresholds and the fallbacks.

body.label: Handling failing calls
head: Habit
Protects against
Zotato example
rows: Menu call gets 300 ms of a 2 s screen budget
Order status fetch: 3 tries, 1–4 s apart, randomised
Payment for order 9101 charged once however often it's retried
Waiting on, and piling onto, a dead dependency
Maps API down: ETA from distance

items: When you draw a call to another service or provider, say what happens if it is slow or down: the timeout, the retry policy and the fallback.
For any write that might be retried, especially payments and orders, say how you make it idempotent.
When asked about reliability or a dependency failing, describe a circuit breaker and what the user sees while it is open.
Watch for retry storms: 'retries are limited, backed off with jitter, and done at one layer only'.

body.x: Backoff and breakers are the caller's side. The overloaded service can protect itself too, by refusing work it can't finish in time: once its queue is longer than it can clear within the callers' timeouts, answering 503 quickly is better than accepting requests that will time out anyway, because a fast refusal costs almost nothing and a slow failure costs as much as a success.

Good shedding refuses the least important work first: during a dinner rush, Zotato would rather drop recommendation requests than order placements. Combined with clients that back off on 503, this lets a system run at its limit without collapsing.
